title: Brent Posts Biggest Weekly Drop Since 2020 on Iran Peace Hopes
content: Crude oil tumbled through the week, with Brent closing Friday around $98.32 a barrel and US WTI near $90.83, leaving Brent down roughly 17% on the week — its steepest weekly fall since the pandemic shock of 2020. The slide came as traders read the Democratic midterm sweep as raising political pressure for a negotiated settlement with Iran that could return Gulf barrels to the market. Continued tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz kept a floor under prices, with no ceasefire yet confirmed.
summary: Brent crude fell about 17% on the week to near $98 as hopes of an Iran settlement eased the geopolitical risk premium.
context:
• Brent had traded above $110 earlier in the period as attacks on Gulf shipping stoked fears of a supply disruption.

• A months-long Middle East conflict involving Iran had built a sizeable war-risk premium into crude prices.

• OPEC+ core producers left December output targets unchanged, with the full 21-member group due to meet on 29 November to set 2027 policy.
happened:
• Brent settled Friday near $98.32 and WTI near $90.83, with Brent down about 17% on the week, the biggest weekly loss since 2020.

• Markets interpreted the US election result as increasing pressure for an Iran deal that could free up additional Gulf exports.

• Reports of fresh tanker attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz limited the decline and underscored that normal shipping had not resumed.
implications:
• A durable de-escalation could unwind more of the risk premium and expose the market to a potential 2027 supply surplus.

• Any breakdown in talks or renewed Hormuz disruption risks a sharp snap-back above $100, with one analyst putting the odds of renewed fighting high.

• The 29 November OPEC+ meeting becomes a pivotal event for 2027 quotas and the group's response to softer prices.
importance:
• Energy prices feed directly into headline inflation and central-bank rate expectations, amplifying the cross-asset read-through.

• Lower crude eases input costs for consumers and industry but squeezes energy-sector earnings and producer-nation budgets.

• The move shows how quickly a geopolitical premium can deflate, raising two-way risk for commodity and equity investors alike.

title: Bitcoin Slides to Mid-$70,000s as Spot ETFs Bleed Cash
content: Bitcoin changed hands around $75,800 by Friday, roughly 40% below its January record, after a volatile week that saw it spike above $80,000 following the US midterms before rolling over. US spot bitcoin ETFs were a key drag, shedding about $430m on Thursday alone and more than $1.2bn across the week's early sessions as the broader risk-off tone in AI-linked equities spilled into digital assets. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index sat at 28, firmly in 'fear' territory.
summary: Bitcoin fell back to around $75,800 as US spot ETFs recorded heavy weekly outflows and risk appetite soured.
context:
• Crypto has traded in close sympathy with high-beta technology shares through 2026, amplifying moves when equity risk appetite turns.

• Spot bitcoin ETFs have become a marginal source of demand, so swings in their flows now move the underlying price.

• Bitcoin remains far below its January peak above $120,000, having ground lower through the autumn alongside stretched growth equities.
happened:
• Bitcoin briefly topped $80,000 on 4 November after the midterm results before sliding to a weekly low near $74,900 on 6 November.

• US spot bitcoin ETFs saw net outflows of about $430m on 5 November, with weekly redemptions topping $1.2bn.

• By 7 November the price sat around $75,800, roughly 40% below its all-time high, with sentiment gauges signalling fear.
implications:
• Sustained ETF redemptions would drain a pillar of demand and leave the market more exposed to leveraged selling.

• Continued correlation with AI equities means a deeper tech sell-off could drag crypto lower still.

• A decisive break of recent support risks triggering further liquidations across leveraged positions.
importance:
• ETF flows have turned bitcoin into a cleaner barometer of institutional risk appetite than in prior cycles.

• The sell-off tests the thesis that crypto can decouple from equities during stress.

• Large drawdowns reverberate across miners, exchanges and crypto-linked equities.

title: Nikkei Enters Bear Market as AI Rout Sweeps Asia
content: Asian equities were hammered on Friday as Wall Street's AI-led sell-off rippled across the region. Japan's Nikkei 225 slumped around 6% — its sharpest one-day fall since April 2025 — tipping into a technical bear market more than 20% below its June peak, while South Korea's Kospi fell as much as 8.8% and triggered a circuit breaker and Taiwan's benchmark dropped about 4.5% into bear-market territory. Mainland China held up better, with reports of state-linked buying helping to stabilise the market.
summary: Japan's Nikkei dropped about 6% into a bear market and Korea's Kospi triggered a circuit breaker as the US AI rout hit Asia.
context:
• Asian indices are heavily weighted towards semiconductor and AI-supply-chain names, leaving them acutely exposed to shifts in the US AI trade.

• The Nikkei and Kospi had rallied to records earlier in 2026 on AI and chip optimism, leaving valuations stretched.

• Beijing has repeatedly leaned on state-linked funds to steady domestic equities during bouts of global stress.
happened:
• The Nikkei 225 closed down roughly 6%, its worst session since April 2025, and slid into a bear market.

• South Korea's Kospi fell as much as 8.8%, prompting a trading circuit breaker, while Taiwan's index lost about 4.5%.

• Mainland Chinese indices fell more modestly, around 1%, with reports of state entities stepping in to buy equities.
implications:
• A prolonged repricing of AI capex expectations would hit Asia's chipmakers and their suppliers hardest.

• Circuit breakers and state intervention highlight how fragile sentiment has become across the region.

• Rotation out of AI-supply-chain names and into discounted Chinese internet platforms could persist.
importance:
• Asia's chip and hardware giants are central to the global AI build-out, so regional moves feed back into US and European tech.

• Bear-market thresholds in major indices shape global risk sentiment and fund positioning.

• State buying in China signals official concern about contagion into the real economy.

title: European Stocks Tumble From Records as Tech Rout Goes Global
content: European equities slid on Friday as the global technology sell-off dragged the region lower, with the STOXX 600 off around 1.3% having set a record high only a day earlier. Germany's DAX fell close to 1.9%, France's CAC 40 lost about 1.4% and London's FTSE 100 shed roughly 1%, as semiconductor and AI-exposed names led the retreat. Even after the pullback, the STOXX 600 held a year-to-date gain of more than 10%, comfortably ahead of the S&P 500's roughly 7%.
summary: The STOXX 600 fell about 1.3% from a record high as the US-led tech rout hit European markets, though it still leads the S&P 500 in 2026.
context:
• European indices had rallied to fresh records this autumn on resilient earnings and rotation out of pricier US tech.

• The region's relative underweight to megacap AI names had helped it outperform Wall Street through 2026.

• Friday's move followed what some outlets called the worst US chip sell-off since 2020.
happened:
• The STOXX 600 fell around 1.3% on Friday after closing at a record high on Thursday.

• The DAX dropped close to 1.9% and the FTSE 100 lost about 1%, with chip and AI-linked shares leading declines.

• Despite the slide, the STOXX 600 retained a double-digit year-to-date gain, ahead of the S&P 500.
implications:
• Europe's relative resilience could keep drawing flows if the US AI trade stays under pressure.

• A deeper global tech correction would test whether European outperformance can hold.

• Easing oil prices and lower bond yields offer some offsetting support to European equities.
importance:
• Europe's 2026 outperformance is reshaping global allocation debates away from US megacap dominance.

• Moves in the DAX, CAC and FTSE set the tone for European corporate funding and sentiment.

• The record-to-rout whipsaw underlines how tightly global equities are now linked through the AI trade.

title: Treasuries Rally as Haven Bid and Growth Fears Drive Yields Lower
content: US government bonds rallied as the equity rout sent investors scurrying for safety and revived bets on Federal Reserve easing. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to around 4.86% and the 2-year to about 4.51%, leaving the 10-year down roughly 40 basis points over the past month. With the federal funds target at 3.75–4.00%, traders leaned into the view that a Democratic Congress and signs of a cooling AI capex cycle could slow growth and bring rate cuts back into focus.
summary: Ten-year Treasury yields fell to about 4.86% as a haven bid and softer growth expectations lifted bond prices.
context:
• The Fed's target range stands at 3.75–4.00% after easing through 2026, with the effective rate near 3.88%.

• Bond markets have been weighing sticky services inflation against signs of slowing momentum.

• A divided-government outcome is widely read as limiting large fiscal packages, a modest tailwind for duration.
happened:
• The 10-year yield slipped to roughly 4.86% and the 2-year to about 4.51% as equities sold off.

• The 10-year is down around 40 basis points over the past month, with the curve holding a positive 10s–2s slope near 35 basis points.

• Falling oil prices reinforced the move by easing near-term inflation concerns.
implications:
• Lower yields ease financial conditions and cushion rate-sensitive sectors if the equity sell-off deepens.

• Renewed rate-cut pricing hinges on upcoming inflation and labour data confirming the slowdown.

• A sharp risk rebound or an inflation surprise could quickly reverse the rally.
importance:
• Treasury yields are the anchor for global borrowing costs and equity valuations.

• The haven bid confirms bonds are again hedging equity risk after a volatile stretch.

• Shifts in rate-cut expectations ripple across FX, credit and mortgage markets.

title: Yen Pinned Near 158 as BoJ Hike Bets Build
content: The dollar held firm against the yen, trading around 158.4 on Friday, even as hawkish Bank of Japan signals revived expectations of a December rate rise. Minutes from the BoJ's September meeting pointed to room for further tightening, with one board member flagging scope to accelerate increases, lending the yen some underlying support against a still-elevated US rate backdrop. The euro traded near $1.1165, with softer Eurozone data weighing on the single currency.
summary: USD/JPY hovered near 158.4 as hawkish BoJ minutes stoked December hike bets, while the euro traded around $1.1165.
context:
• The yen has stayed weak through 2026 as wide US-Japan rate differentials favoured the dollar.

• The BoJ has been cautiously normalising policy after years of ultra-loose settings.

• Japanese officials have repeatedly warned they stand ready to act against disorderly currency moves.
happened:
• USD/JPY traded around 158.4 on 6 November, little moved despite the broader risk-off tone.

• September BoJ minutes reinforced expectations of further tightening, with a December hike seen as a live possibility.

• Japan's finance minister reiterated readiness to coordinate currency policy with Washington.
implications:
• A December BoJ hike could spark a sharper yen rally and pressure crowded carry trades.

• Persistent US rate advantage may cap yen gains even as the BoJ turns more hawkish.

• Further yen weakness past 158 raises the risk of official intervention.
importance:
• USD/JPY is a key barometer of global rate differentials and carry-trade risk.

• Yen moves ripple through Japanese equities, exporters and global funding markets.

• A disorderly unwind of yen shorts has historically amplified cross-asset volatility.

title: Gold Slips From Highs Even as Equities Tumble
content: Gold eased to around $4,070 an ounce by Friday, slipping a few tenths of a percent on the day after touching roughly $4,150 earlier in the week. The pullback, even against a backdrop of plunging equities, reflected a mix of deleveraging, a firmer dollar and sliding oil prices that cooled near-term inflation fears. Goldman Sachs was reported to have trimmed its end-2026 gold target to around $4,150 an ounce.
summary: Gold eased to about $4,070 an ounce as deleveraging and falling oil offset the usual haven bid during the equity rout.
context:
• Gold has had a powerful 2026, hitting records above $5,000 earlier in the year amid geopolitical and rate uncertainty.

• Bullion often sells off alongside risk assets during acute deleveraging, as investors raise cash.

• Lower oil prices this week eased the inflation backdrop that had underpinned part of gold's rally.
happened:
• Spot gold traded around $4,070 an ounce on 6 November, down modestly on the day after nearing $4,150 earlier in the week.

• A firmer dollar and sharply lower crude prices weighed on the metal.

• Goldman Sachs was reported to have cut its end-2026 gold forecast to about $4,150 from a higher prior estimate.
implications:
• If the equity sell-off deepens into a broader deleveraging, gold could stay choppy before any renewed haven bid.

• Falling oil and a stronger dollar may keep near-term pressure on the metal.

• Lower real yields from the bond rally would, over time, offer support.
importance:
• Gold's behaviour during the rout tests its reputation as a crisis hedge versus a liquidity source.

• Bullion remains a key gauge of real-rate expectations and dollar strength.

• Analyst forecast cuts shape positioning among funds and central-bank buyers.

title: Chip Stocks Crater as AI Capex 'War of Attrition' Fears Bite
content: Semiconductor and data-centre shares led Thursday's rout, with Nvidia sinking about 9% and AMD plunging roughly 17% as investors questioned the durability of the AI build-out. Data-centre names such as Astera Labs and Applied Digital fell around 11% apiece, in what some outlets branded the worst US chip sell-off since 2020, before a tentative rebound Friday lifted Nvidia about 2.8%. The sell-off crystallised fears that a Democratic Congress could slow data-centre construction while the sheer scale of AI capex draws fresh scrutiny.
summary: Nvidia fell about 9% and AMD around 17% as investors questioned AI capex sustainability in the worst chip sell-off since 2020.
context:
• AI chipmakers have driven much of the US market's 2026 gains, leaving the group richly valued and crowded.

• Commentary has increasingly focused on how AI data-centre build-outs are being financed and whether returns justify the spend.

• The midterm result raised the prospect of tighter AI regulation and a slower construction pipeline.
happened:
• Nvidia dropped about 9% on Thursday and AMD fell roughly 17%, with data-centre names like Astera Labs and Applied Digital off around 11%.

• Analysts described the AI data-centre build-out as a 'war of attrition', concentrating strain in the riskiest corners of AI financing.

• Chip stocks stabilised Friday, with Nvidia bouncing about 2.8%, though the group stayed well below its October peaks.
implications:
• A sustained repricing of AI capex expectations would weigh on chipmakers, hardware suppliers and power and data-centre plays.

• Scrutiny of AI financing structures could tighten credit for the most leveraged build-out players.

• Any softening in hyperscaler spending guidance would deepen the correction.
importance:
• Semiconductors are the epicentre of the AI trade that has powered global equities.

• The debate over capex returns speaks directly to whether the AI rally is sustainable.

• Concentrated index weightings mean chip swings move the entire market.

title: Nasdaq Enters Correction as Midterm Shock Triggers AI Sell-Off
content: Wall Street suffered its worst session since April 2025 on Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite plunging 5.5% into correction territory, the S&P 500 falling 4.4% and the Dow shedding more than 1,800 points. The slide wiped close to $3tn off S&P 500 companies as investors reassessed the AI trade following a Democratic midterm sweep that stoked fears of tighter regulation and a slower data-centre build-out. A tentative rebound Friday left the S&P 500 up about 0.3%, but the index still ended the week lower.
summary: The Nasdaq fell 5.5% into correction and the S&P 500 lost 4.4% as a Democratic midterm sweep triggered an AI-led rout.
context:
• Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, securing their largest House majority since 2008 and control of the Senate.

• Markets initially rallied on the result, with the Dow posting its best post-midterm day in decades on hopes of divided-government gridlock.

• Sentiment reversed sharply as investors focused on risks to the AI build-out from tighter regulation.
happened:
• The Nasdaq fell 5.5% on Thursday into correction, more than 10% below its early-October record, while the S&P 500 lost 4.4% and the Dow dropped over 1,800 points.

• The rout erased close to $3tn in S&P 500 market value in the worst day since April 2025.

• Stocks steadied Friday, with the S&P 500 up roughly 0.3% and the Nasdaq about 1.1% higher, though the week closed in the red.
implications:
• The correction raises the risk of further de-risking if AI-capex doubts and policy uncertainty persist.

• Divided government may constrain fiscal stimulus while sharpening the regulatory debate over AI.

• Volatility is likely to stay elevated as investors reassess megacap concentration.
importance:
• US megacap tech anchors global equity benchmarks, so a Nasdaq correction reverberates worldwide.

• The episode shows how quickly a political surprise can reprice the market's dominant theme.

• Concentration risk in AI leaders leaves indices vulnerable to sharp, broad drawdowns.
